The small red scorpionfish Scorpaena notata is a scorpionfish species distributed widely across the Mediterranean Sea and adjacent eastern Atlantic waters. Field surveys conducted in the Gulf of Lions report that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal eggs after an incubation period of approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days] at 14.6 °C [T = 14.6 °C]. At the moment of eclosion, these prolarvae possess a modest wet weight at birth of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a mass that supports an entirely lecithotrophic existence until the onset of exogenous feeding. This brief embryonic phase is typical of scorpaenids, whose pelagic larval duration is relatively compressed compared to many other teleost families. The yolk absorption stage proceeds rapidly, with first exogenous feeding usually commencing within a few days of hatching, at which point the larvae begin actively foraging on small copepods and other zooplankton.

As the planktonic larvae grow and develop through the flexion and postflexion stages, they undergo a pronounced larval metamorphosis that culminates in benthic settlement, after which the post-metamorphic juveniles adopt a cryptic, demersal lifestyle. Growth during this juvenile phase is initially rapid, but it slows considerably as individuals approach their ultimate total length of 26 centimeters [Li = 26 centimeters]. This asymptotic size, which represents the maximum recorded total length in adults from the western Mediterranean, is a key determinant of reproductive potential. Females attain sexual maturity, defined by the onset of vitellogenesis and the presence of maturing oocytes in the ovaries, at a total length at puberty of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters]. This size threshold is reached after approximately one to two years of growth, depending on local food availability and thermal conditions.

Reproductive activity in Scorpaena notata is strongly influenced by water temperature, with spawning occurring primarily during the late spring and early summer months. At a sustained temperature of 14.6 °C [T = 14.6 °C], detailed aquarium observations have documented that individual females release between 85 and 95 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 85 and 95 eggs per spawning event], with a typical spawning frequency of approximately one event every 24 hours [F_R_i = approximately one event every 24 hours] over the course of the breeding season. This high-frequency spawning strategy yields a substantial daily reproductive output, though the actual number of clutches produced per female in a single season is contingent upon energetic reserves and the availability of suitable rocky crevices for egg deposition. Males exhibit no parental care beyond the initial deposition of sperm during gamete release.

The ultimate wet weight of Scorpaena notata reaches approximately 236 grams [Wwi = approximately 236 grams] in fully grown adults, a value derived from length-weight regressions based on extensive specimen collections from the Balearic Sea. This adult body mass represents a more than 130,000-fold increase over the 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams] recorded at hatching, underscoring the remarkable growth trajectory of this species. The weight-length relationship for this species, with an exponent close to 3.0, indicates that growth is approximately isometric, meaning body shape and condition remain relatively constant across size classes. Gravid females at the peak of the spawning season may exceed this average mass by ten to fifteen percent due to the accumulation of hydrated oocytes within the ovarian lumen, a temporary condition that diminishes rapidly after oviposition.

Longevity estimates for the small red scorpionfish, derived from otolith increment analysis of wild-caught individuals, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately eight years [am = approximately eight years] at 14.6 °C [T = 14.6 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, combined with the iteroparous reproductive strategy and the capacity for repeated spawning bouts within a single season, suggests that lifetime fecundity can be substantial for this species. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in condition factor and a reduction in the number of viable oocytes produced per spawning event, though some females captured at ages exceeding seven years still exhibit active gonadal recrudescence. The interplay between thermal regime and food availability ultimately governs the pace of life history in this scorpionfish, as in many other Mediterranean rocky-reef teleosts.
